title: Jeremiah 13:15–27
context: Jeremiah 13:15–27 gathers several appeals and laments. In 13:15–17 a speaker, most naturally Jeremiah, calls the people to hear, not to be proud, and to “Give glory to the LORD your God” before darkness comes (compare Joshua 7:19), and says that if they will not hear, “my soul will weep in secret for your pride” (13:17; compare 9:1; 14:17). In 13:18–19 a word is addressed to the king and the queen mother, whose crowns have come down; many readers identify them with Jehoiachin and his mother Nehushta, who were taken to Babylon (2 Kings 24:8, 12, 15; compare Jeremiah 22:26; 29:2), though the passage does not name them and some suggest a different king. In 13:20–27 Jerusalem is addressed directly: enemies come from the north (compare 1:14), those she cultivated as allies will rule over her, and the LORD says, “This is your lot, the portion measured to you from me” (13:25). The LORD is named as the speaker in 13:25, and the first person of 13:26–27 is most naturally his voice, while the speaker in 13:20–23 is not named and may be the LORD or the prophet. The language of uncovered skirts (13:22, 26) is an image of public disgrace for a people who have been unfaithful, and these notes treat it soberly. Verse 23 asks, “Can the Ethiopian change his skin, or the leopard his spots?” In context it describes Judah’s deeply ingrained habit of doing evil; later Christian readers have also used it in discussions of human inability, which the notes describe without a verdict, pointing to the existing boxes at Genesis 6:5, Romans 3:11, and Ephesians 2:1 (compare Jeremiah 17:9). The chapter ends with a lament over Jerusalem’s unfaithfulness and the question, “How long will it yet be?” (13:27).

verses.text: Hear, and give ear. Don’t be proud, for the LORD has spoken.
verses.arminianNotes: The prophet calls, “Hear, and give ear. Don’t be proud, for the LORD has spoken.” Arminian readers note the urgent appeal to listen, which implies that a response is still possible, and they see Jeremiah pleading with the people before the judgment he has announced comes.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same appeal and read it as the means God uses to call his people to humility. They observe that pride is again named as the obstacle to hearing, linking this appeal with the ruined pride of 13:9, a point both traditions share.

verses.text: Give glory to the LORD your God, before he causes darkness, and before your feet stumble on the dark mountains, and while you look for light, he turns it into the shadow of death, and makes it deep darkness.
verses.arminianNotes: The prophet says, “Give glory to the LORD your God, before he causes darkness”. Arminian readers note the echo of Joshua 7:19, where Achan is urged to give glory to God and confess, and they see the verse as a call to repent while there is still time.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same echo, named here without harmonizing, and read giving glory to God as acknowledging his rightness and confessing sin. They observe that the images of stumbling on dark mountains and light turned to deep darkness describe the danger of delay.

verses.text: But if you will not hear it, my soul will weep in secret for your pride. My eye will weep bitterly, and run down with tears, because the LORD’s flock has been taken captive.
verses.arminianNotes: The prophet says, “But if you will not hear it, my soul will weep in secret for your pride.” Arminian readers note Jeremiah’s deep sorrow for his people, and they compare 9:1 and 14:17, named without harmonizing, seeing a prophet who grieves even as he warns.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same sorrow and observe that the prophet’s tears reflect God’s own grief over his people (compare 12:7). They read the verse as showing that faithful proclamation of judgment is joined with love, which both traditions see as a model for ministry.

verses.text: Say to the king and to the queen mother, “Humble yourselves. Sit down, for your crowns have come down, even the crown of your glory.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD tells the prophet to say to the king and the queen mother, “Humble yourselves. Sit down, for your crowns have come down”. Arminian readers note that many identify them with Jehoiachin and Nehushta (2 Kings 24:8, 12, 15), though the passage does not name them, and they hold the identification loosely.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the common identification and compare Jeremiah 22:26 and 29:2, named here without harmonizing, while observing that some suggest a different king. They read the call to humility as a word to Judah’s highest rulers that God’s judgment reaches the throne.

verses.text: The cities of the South are shut up, and there is no one to open them. Judah is carried away captive: all of them. They are wholly carried away captive.
verses.arminianNotes: The cities of the South are shut up, and Judah is carried away captive, all of it. Arminian readers note that the South here is the Negev, the southern region of Judah, and they read the verse as a vivid announcement of exile, spoken as though it had already happened.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same picture of complete exile and read the language as prophetic certainty about God’s coming judgment. They observe that the phrase wholly carried away may be poetic emphasis, since other passages speak of some remaining in the land, and they do not press it literally.

verses.text: Lift up your eyes, and see those who come from the north. Where is the flock that was given to you, your beautiful flock?
verses.arminianNotes: The prophet or the LORD says, “Lift up your eyes, and see those who come from the north.” Arminian readers note the echo of 1:14, where evil breaks out from the north, and they hear the question about the beautiful flock as a rebuke to leaders who failed to care for the people.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same echo and observe that the speaker is not named here, so the voice may be the LORD’s or the prophet’s. They read the question about the flock as holding Jerusalem’s leaders accountable for the people entrusted to them, a point both traditions share.

verses.text: What will you say when he sets over you as head those whom you have yourself taught to be friends to you? Won’t sorrows take hold of you, as of a woman in travail?
verses.arminianNotes: The speaker asks what Jerusalem will say when those she taught to be friends are set over her as head. Arminian readers note that the allies she cultivated may become her rulers, perhaps a reference to Babylon, though the identification is not certain, and they see the folly of trusting foreign powers.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same irony and read the comparison with a woman in labor as an image of sudden, unavoidable distress. They observe that the verse warns against seeking security in political alliances rather than in God, a warning both traditions draw from the prophets.

verses.text: If you say in your heart, “Why have these things come on me?” Your skirts are uncovered because of the greatness of your iniquity, and your heels suffer violence.
verses.arminianNotes: Jerusalem asks, “Why have these things come on me?” and is told that her disgrace comes “because of the greatness of your iniquity”. Arminian readers read the language of uncovered skirts as an image of public shame, and they see the answer as tracing judgment to her own sin.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise read the image soberly as public disgrace and exposure before the nations. They observe that the verse answers the people’s question directly: what they suffer is not random but the consequence of covenant unfaithfulness, which both traditions affirm.

verses.text: Can the Ethiopian change his skin, or the leopard his spots? Then may you also do good, who are accustomed to do evil.
verses.arminianNotes: The prophet asks, “Can the Ethiopian change his skin, or the leopard his spots?” In context it speaks of Judah’s ingrained habit of evil. Arminian readers often add that prevenient grace, given before conversion, enables a response no sinner could make alone, and point to the existing box at Romans 3:11.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise begin with the primary sense of Judah’s deep habit, then often use the verse to illustrate human inability apart from regenerating grace (compare Jeremiah 17:9). They point to the existing boxes at Genesis 6:5, Romans 3:11, and Ephesians 2:1 rather than opening a new contrast, and reach no verdict here.

verses.text: “Therefore I will scatter them as the stubble that passes away by the wind of the wilderness.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says, “Therefore I will scatter them as the stubble that passes away by the wind of the wilderness.” Arminian readers note the image of light chaff blown away, and they see it as a picture of exile in which a people who would not hear are dispersed among the nations.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same image of scattering and read it as the outworking of covenant judgment. They observe that the wind of the wilderness may evoke the hot desert wind, and they read the verse as the certain result of persistent refusal to turn back to God.

verses.text: This is your lot, the portion measured to you from me,” says the LORD, “because you have forgotten me, and trusted in falsehood.”
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says, “This is your lot, the portion measured to you from me”, because the people have forgotten him and trusted in falsehood. Arminian readers note that the lot is measured in response to their forgetting and false trust, which they see as freely chosen.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the language of a measured portion stresses that the judgment comes from God’s hand and is fitting to the offense. They read forgetting God and trusting in falsehood as the root of Judah’s sin, a diagnosis both traditions share.

verses.text: Therefore I will also uncover your skirts on your face, and your shame will appear.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says, “Therefore I will also uncover your skirts on your face, and your shame will appear.” Arminian readers read this soberly as an image of public disgrace in the sight of the nations, and they see it as the consequence of a people’s long unfaithfulness to their God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise read the image soberly as exposure and humiliation in judgment. They observe that the verse uses the language of covenant unfaithfulness found elsewhere in the prophets, and they read it as showing that hidden sin will be brought into the open.

verses.text: I have seen your abominations, even your adulteries and your neighing, the lewdness of your prostitution, on the hills in the field. Woe to you, Jerusalem! You will not be made clean. How long will it yet be?”
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says, “I have seen your abominations”, and laments, “Woe to you, Jerusalem! You will not be made clean. How long will it yet be?” Arminian readers note that the closing question implies a longing for Jerusalem’s cleansing, and they hear grief as well as judgment in it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same question and read the imagery of unfaithfulness on the hills as a picture of idolatry (compare 5:8), described soberly. They observe that the question how long leaves room for future cleansing, a hope Jeremiah develops later in the book, which both traditions share.
